extracted.intended_audience: public relations practitioners, students, and educators
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on applying communication theory to the research, design, writing, media selection, and evaluation of public relations materials and campaigns. Emphasizes audience analysis, choice of theory, message design, and medium selection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of communication theory in PR writing
rubrics_metrics.description: Theory provides an important foundation for any type of public relations writing. It provides a framework for turning ideas into plans and plans into campaigns, encouraging strategic and critical thinking within well-defined parameters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use theory to understand, research, and write about an organization or organizational problem; without theory 'we have no avenue to travel' — theory should guide problem definition, research, message design, media choice, and evaluation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Problem identification and narrowing
rubrics_metrics.description: When dealing with any kind of public relations activities you as writer must identify and narrow the problem so that only one specific problem is addressed at any given time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Research to define and narrow the problem to a manageable size (example: high employee absenteeism — investigate environmental, personnel, morale, management, and information-distribution causes); failure to properly define the problem undermines solution design.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conduct internal and external situation analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: An analysis of the internal and external situations requires an examination of all elements of the organization — departments, employees, managers, administrators and their relationships — to properly form an idea of the organization, its culture and its functions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine interrelations, dependencies, feedback loops and environmental interactions before designing messages or interventions; research results should drive strategy (case-study examples included).

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience analysis / understanding targeted publics
rubrics_metrics.description: The public relations writer must design a message tailored to meet the needs of that public or publics. Understanding how people perceive, conceptualize information, and integrate it into their cognitive systems is essential.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determine publics' beliefs, attitudes, involvement and media habits; tailor content, tone, and complexity accordingly (e.g., university professors vs. CEOs vs. parents).

rubrics_metrics.name: Quality of message presentation (style, format, mechanics, presentation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Appropriate message content and organization, audience analysis, and quality of message presentation (i.e., style, format, mechanics, presentation) are central concerns when writing PR materials.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adapt writing style and format to the medium (tighter writing for electronic media, journalistic style for magazines, polished prose for profiles); pay attention to mechanics and professional presentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of General Systems Theory (GST)
rubrics_metrics.description: General Systems Theory conceptualizes organizations as interrelated parts forming a whole and is adapted to public relations activities and success.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply GST to view the organization holistically; ensure interventions consider systemic effects and feedback rather than isolated fixes.

rubrics_metrics.name: GST — Wholeness
rubrics_metrics.description: A system constitutes a whole; all parts are interrelated and any change in one part affects the whole system.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When designing PR actions, evaluate consequences across the organization; avoid isolated changes that may have unintended systemic impacts.

rubrics_metrics.name: GST — Interdependence
rubrics_metrics.description: All parts of a system are intertwined and affect one another; mutual interaction produces results different from isolated parts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coordinate communication across departments and stakeholders; leverage information exchange for coordinated solutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: GST — Hierarchy
rubrics_metrics.description: Systems create levels of increasing complexity (administrators, managers, subordinates, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize organizational levels when planning messages and channels; match messages to decision-making levels and influencers.

rubrics_metrics.name: GST — Self-regulation and control
rubrics_metrics.description: Systems behave according to rules and goals and adapt based on feedback.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Build mechanisms for feedback and self-correction into campaigns (e.g., committees, suggestion boxes, staff reports).

rubrics_metrics.name: GST — Interchange with the environment
rubrics_metrics.description: Systems exchange information with their environment; that interchange provides the basis for successful or unsuccessful relationships with communities and publics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plan outward-facing communication and listening strategies; maintain environmental scanning to inform PR tactics.

rubrics_metrics.name: GST — Balance
rubrics_metrics.description: Systems must sense and adjust to deviations from norms or standards to maintain balance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use communication to restore balance when tensions arise; monitor indicators and act early to prevent escalation.

rubrics_metrics.name: GST — Change and adaptability
rubrics_metrics.description: Organizations undergo internal or external changes and must adapt (e.g., employee departures, reorganizations).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design flexible communication plans that can pivot in response to changing conditions and stakeholder needs.

rubrics_metrics.name: GST — Equifinality
rubrics_metrics.description: A particular final state may be accomplished in many ways from different starting points.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be open to multiple strategic paths to achieve objectives (e.g., produce a newsletter in-house, assign reporters, or outsource); choose approach fitting resources and culture.

rubrics_metrics.name: Information processing as predictor of attitudes
rubrics_metrics.description: When new information is processed, a person's cognitive system must change to accommodate it; this reorganization can lead to attitude change (persuasion).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess how target publics process information so messages can be packaged for comprehension, acceptance, and elaboration; anticipate complementing or contradicting existing beliefs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Yale Attitude Approach — Source, Message, Channel, Receiver variables
rubrics_metrics.description: Persuasive messages are stimuli mediated by cognition; primary variables related to change are Source, Message, Channel and Receiver.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate and design each variable: source credibility; message interest, clarity, acceptability; channel modality and distractions; receiver traits and involvement (examples discussed).

rubrics_metrics.name: Channel selection considerations (noise, modality, availability)
rubrics_metrics.description: Channel effectiveness depends on level of distraction and medium; combined visual and auditory modes (e.g., TV) can be more effective than single-mode channels, but channel choice is constrained by resources and availability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Match channel to audience access and budget; consider rural/urban availability and potential distractions; multimodal approaches may increase impact if resources allow.

rubrics_metrics.name: Receiver persuadability factors
rubrics_metrics.description: Persuadability is influenced by personality factors (age, gender), and degree of interest/involvement; higher involvement often reduces susceptibility to persuasion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Segment audiences by involvement and background; expect differing processing and time needed to change attitudes (example: entrenched employees are harder to persuade).

rubrics_metrics.name: Designing persuasive strategies — Social Learning Theory
rubrics_metrics.description: Learning is social: people observe, emulate, and integrate behaviors; if rewarded, behaviors and related attitudes are adopted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use modeling and reward structures in campaigns (e.g., encourage desired behaviors via visible role models and incentives; Potek salary-cut/reward case study demonstrates modeling and reward).

rubrics_metrics.name: Designing persuasive strategies — Social Exchange Theory
rubrics_metrics.description: People dislike indebtedness; relationships seek equitable exchanges of resources. Inequity produces tension that prompts communication or termination of relationships.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design programs that create equitable resource exchange (e.g., WHJ bank's school program provides training to teachers and publicity/customers to bank). Use communication to restore perceived equity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Designing persuasive strategies — Two-way symmetrical communication
rubrics_metrics.description: Symmetrical communication occurs when communicators share control of the exchange; two-way interaction and feedback are essential for positive internal and external relationships.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor two-way, dialogic strategies for long-term relationship building (Vivian's Country Club case study illustrates surveying, responding, and repairing relationships to grow membership).

rubrics_metrics.name: Defining publics — Coorientation model (awareness & shared interests)
rubrics_metrics.description: A public is a group aware of shared interests; key elements are degree of self-awareness and orientation toward shared interests. Communication increases mutual understanding even without agreement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify publics by shared interests and awareness; facilitate communication between groups (e.g., employees and management) to increase perceived agreement and ease persuasion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Defining publics — Elaboration-Likelihood Model (ELM)
rubrics_metrics.description: People are persuaded by thinking about and elaborating on a message; individuals vary in knowledge and involvement so message processing differs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tailor messages for central vs peripheral processing; provide differing message complexity for experts vs novices; multiple, audience-specific messages may be necessary (Clorise's Respiratory Association case used dual messages for general public and children).

rubrics_metrics.name: Selecting media — audience media usage and credibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider what audience you are trying to reach and what you know about its media usage patterns and the credibility ratings for each medium.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Research media habits and credibility perceptions of target publics; do not assume broad reach or credibility of a medium (example: business people value newspapers while others rely on TV).

rubrics_metrics.name: Selecting media — timing (when you need to reach the audience)
rubrics_metrics.description: When do you need to reach this audience in order for your message to be effective? Media deadlines and timeliness affect medium suitability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Match medium to timing constraints (e.g., magazines may not suit urgent needs; memos/phone calls or in-house letters may be better for quick corporate decisions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Selecting media — cost and budget constraints
rubrics_metrics.description: How much do you need to spend to reach your intended audience, and how much can you actually afford? Budget considerations influence the final decision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize objectives vs. cost; coming in under budget enhances perceived success. Consider donated airtime, community partnerships, and low-cost channels when appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selecting media — maximize reach at lowest cost (bottom-line choice)
rubrics_metrics.description: Which medium reaches the broadest segment of your target audience at the lowest cost? This often yields the bottom-line choice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare reach-per-dollar across candidate media; combine with credibility and timing factors to select media that best meet objectives and budget.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selecting media — credibility vs cost tradeoff
rubrics_metrics.description: Which medium has the highest credibility and what does it cost? Credibility affects audience perception and can influence campaign success.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balance credibility and cost; sometimes paying more for a credible medium is justified for discriminating audiences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selecting media — deliverability within time constraints
rubrics_metrics.description: Which medium will deliver your message within the time constraints necessary for it to be effective?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess lead times, production schedules, and distribution speed; choose channels that meet the campaign's time needs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selecting media — single medium vs media mix
rubrics_metrics.description: Should a single medium be used or a combination of complementary media (media mix)?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider audience complexity — unique individuals do not receive messages the same way; use complementary media to increase coverage and reinforcement when appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Functions and desirable characteristics of theory
rubrics_metrics.description: Important characteristics/functions of theory: (1) presents a systematic view of observed phenomena; (2) specifies relations among variables; (3) specifies how variables are related; (4) explains past and/or present behavior; (5) predicts future behavior.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose theories that provide systematic explanation and predictive power; use theory to both guide practice and to be tested/confirmed by practical outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate campaign results and the 'bottom line'
rubrics_metrics.description: Effective evaluation of efforts and understanding the bottom line are essential; students/practitioners should micro-manage activities toward purposeful achievement and evaluate outcomes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design measurable evaluations (e.g., media coverage increases, sales declines, awareness metrics) as part of campaign planning (case-study results provided: media coverage %, sales declines, awareness increases).
